text:
Who sees which button? Let users choose, and the two groups differ before the test even starts. Here's how far apart they sit on ten traits. Age, income, prior use... and two that nobody recorded, like motivation. Flip a coin for each user instead, and every gap shrinks to noise. Even the two nobody measured. The coin doesn't know what it's balancing, so it balances everything. That's what lets a test say the button CAUSED the change. Two more decisions, before anyone clicks.

How many users? To catch ten percent rising to twelve, with eighty percent power, you need about three thousand eight hundred per arm. And no peeking. Here's a test where both arms are identical. There's nothing to find. Recompute its p-value after every hundred visitors, and it wanders... dipping under point oh five, twice. Stop at the first dip, and you've shipped noise. At the planned eight thousand, it reads point one nine. So set the number, and look once, at the end.

Here's a finished test, with six thousand users in each arm. Five hundred and seventy-nine bought with the old button. Seven hundred and two with the new. That's nine point six five percent against eleven point seven. A lift of two points... about a fifth more sales. Its ninety-five percent interval runs from about one point to three, and the p-value is three in ten thousand. Report all four together: the lift, its interval, the p-value, and an effect size. Never the p-value alone.

Then decide, on two questions. Is it significant? Yes. The whole interval sits above zero. And is it big enough to matter? That one's about money, not math. A big enough test makes even eight percent rising to eight point oh two significant. It's real... and worthless. Significance gives you permission to look at the size. It doesn't tell you to ship.
